Ball 3 alone begins its life in the third slot with certainty, and a ball that starts in that slot has the highest possible chance of eventual piston ejection (17⁄27 ≈ 0.63). No later-numbered ball is guaranteed that advantageous starting position, and balls 1 and 2 start in less-favorable slots. Hence selecting ball 3 maximizes the probability of winning.
When your chosen ball first appears on the three-slot platform, the slot it occupies determines its fate.

Let p1, p2, p3 be the probabilities that a ball eventually gets piston-ejected (win) when it first occupies slot 1, 2, 3 respectively.

• From slot 1: win if piston 1 fires (prob 1/3); otherwise it is released.  p1 = 1/3.

• From slot 2: win instantly if piston 2 fires (1/3); otherwise the ball moves to slot 1.  p2 = 1/3 + (2/3)p1 = 5/9.

• From slot 3: win instantly if piston 3 fires (1/3); if piston 2 fires it jumps to slot 1; if piston 1 fires it moves to slot 2.  p3 = 1/3 + (1/3)p1 + (1/3)p2 = 17/27.

Thus p3 > p2 > p1.

At the moment you must choose, balls 1, 2, 3 are already on the platform in slots 1, 2, 3 respectively.  All later balls enter only after the first piston fires and will start in slot 2 or 3 with lower average success probability than p3.

Therefore the ball now sitting in slot 3—ball number 3—has the greatest chance of being ejected by a piston, so it maximizes your probability of winning.

Let the host’s (unknown) coin counts, after they are put in ascending order, be x1≤x2≤x3 with x1+x2+x3=30 and with one difference of 6.  The smallest possible middle value is 6 (distribution 0,6,24) and the smallest possible largest value is 12 (distribution 6,12,12).  

Bob picks non-decreasing guesses g1≤g2≤g3.  Because the host can permute the boxes adversarially, the host will always match Bob’s largest guess with x1, his middle guess with x2 and his smallest guess with x3.  Bob’s winnings are therefore
  P0 = g1 + g2 if g2≤6    (host chooses 0,6,24)
  P6 = g1 + (g2 if g2≤12) + (g3 if g3≤6) (host chooses 6,12,12).
The host will pay Bob only the smaller of P0 and P6.

1.  If g2>6, then P0 = g1, and P6 ≤ g1 + g2.  Hence the guaranteed amount is g1.
    The biggest g1 that can be guaranteed in all cases is 12 (because x3 can be as low as 12), so this gives at most 12 coins.
2.  If g2≤6, then Bob’s guarantee is P0 = g1+g2.  Since g1≤g2≤6, the maximum of g1+g2 is achieved at g1=g2=6, giving 12 coins.

Thus no strategy can force more than 12 coins, and Bob can attain this bound by guessing 6 for each box (or any non-decreasing triple with g1=g2=6).

Each coin is worth $1,000, so the least amount of money Bob can still guarantee himself under optimal play is 12×1,000.
Let the host’s (unknown to Bob) coin counts, arranged in non-decreasing order, be x₁≤x₂≤x₃, with x₁+x₂+x₃ =30 and one difference exactly six.  The list of all possible ordered triples gives the following twelve distinct sorted triples: (0,6,24),(1,7,22),(2,8,20),(3,9,18),(4,10,16),(5,11,14),(6,12,12),(6,9,15),(7,10,13),(8,8,14),(2,11,17),(0,12,18).  Hence   min x₁ = 0 and min x₂ = 6.  Bob submits three guesses g₁≥g₂≥g₃.  The host, having already fixed a distribution, can relabel the boxes so that Bob’s largest guess g₁ is matched with the smallest coin pile x₁, g₂ with x₂, and g₃ with x₃.  Bob’s payoff is P = Σ gᵢ·1{gᵢ≤matched x}.  To guarantee a positive payoff on the second and third matches, Bob must keep   g₂ ≤ min x₂ = 6 and g₃ ≤ g₂.  Setting g₂ = g₃ = 6 meets those constraints and yields at least 6+6 = 12 coins in every possible distribution; any larger choice for g₂ would be wiped out by the distribution (0,6,24), and any smaller value would lower the guaranteed total.  The first (largest) guess can be anything, since it is inevitably paired with x₁ which can be 0; choosing it arbitrarily gives no additional guaranteed coins.  Therefore the maximum amount Bob can force, and hence the minimum he is sure to win, is 12 coins, i.e. $12,000.
